strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for human-in-the-loop NLP: how collaborative workflows influence the outputs of interactive qualitative analysis tools. Its emphasis on evaluating complete workflows is useful beyond standalone model evaluation.

The comparison spans three distinct approaches—topic modeling, relational inference, and LLM-based coding—and two contrasting corpora. Using common initial partitions within each system helps control starting conditions.

The evaluation combines document overlap, semantic similarity, and manual assessment of 1,200 document–theme pairs. Double annotation with adjudication and reporting of Krippendorff’s alpha provide useful transparency. The appendices also document interface operations, prompts, and some computational settings.
weaknesses: The design does not isolate collaboration timing. Section 4 compares individual coders with three-person synchronous groups, without consolidating the individual codebooks into an asynchronous team output. Timing is therefore entangled with team size and consensus formation. Some participants also always perform asynchronous coding first, introducing possible learning effects; allocation and time budgets are insufficiently documented. The conclusions should concern the observed group-versus-individual configurations unless stronger controls are introduced.

The statistical evidence does not adequately establish the central claims. Each system has only two synchronous groups and three individual sessions; the synchronous consistency comparison consequently contains only one pair of group codebooks. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying the observational unit or explaining how dependencies among themes, document pairs, and reused participants are handled. Multiple testing is also unaddressed. Session-level results, effect uncertainty, and an analysis respecting these dependencies are necessary before the significance claims can support a Findings recommendation.

The proposed framework needs stronger validation as a measure of qualitative analysis quality. Maximum-similarity alignment can reuse a target theme and is sensitive to codebook granularity. Theme counts, size distributions, and coverage are not adequately reported. Embedding similarity measures semantic compactness, but does not establish interpretive usefulness or thematic validity. Sensitivity analyses and human judgments of theme quality would help justify interpreting higher scores as deeper or clearer analysis.

The correctness evaluation is incomplete and underspecified. Reported human results cover COVID data only. Figure 4 labels its outcome F1, but the paper does not define its calculation, averaging, or reference labels sufficiently. Aggregation across sessions and the estimand implied by uniform sampling over themes also need clarification. Confidence intervals are absent, and alpha = 0.632 indicates meaningful annotation uncertainty. Table 10 additionally reports 0.7–16.1% invalid-label outputs, without clearly explaining their treatment in the evaluation.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the provided appendices. The stated 15 experiments and 33 participants are not mapped clearly across both datasets and repeated participation. Important details are missing, including the exact SBERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, generated codebooks, and selected prompts per session. The interview sample and qualitative analysis procedure are also insufficiently specified to assess the reported experiential themes. A promised release does not resolve these omissions in the current manuscript.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. For Climate, the relational and LLM systems improve intra-theme similarity by only 0.01, which does not substantiate the description of uniformly much more cohesive themes. Explanations involving cognitive load, semantic diversity, and deliberation remain hypotheses because these factors are not isolated. Likewise, broad conclusions about LLM scalability and reliability rest on one 3B model configuration without comparative efficiency measurements. Narrowing these claims, alongside resolving the design and inference concerns, is needed for resubmission.
